title: `this` and Function Context
summary: `this` is decided at call time by how a function is invoked, not where it's defined — four rules cover every case, and arrow functions are the one exception that opts out entirely.

slides.markdown:
More bugs get filed against `this` than against almost any other JS feature, and nearly all of them come from one wrong assumption: that `this` is fixed by where a function is **written**, the way [closures](closures) fix a variable's scope.

It isn't. `this` is resolved at **call time**, based on how the function is invoked — `obj.method()` vs `method()` vs `method.call(x)` vs `new Method()` all set `this` differently for the exact same function body.

Four rules cover every case, plus one deliberate exception: arrow functions don't have their own `this` at all. Get the four rules and the exception solid and every "detached callback loses `this`" bug becomes predictable instead of mysterious.

slides.sectionTitle: `this` is set at the call site
slides.subTitle: Not at the definition site
Default, implicit, explicit, `new`
slides.markdown:
In order of precedence, lowest to highest:

| Rule | Call shape | `this` becomes |
|---|---|---|
| **Default** | `fn()` — bare call | `undefined` in strict mode (the global object in sloppy mode) |
| **Implicit** | `obj.fn()` | `obj` — whatever is left of the dot |
| **Explicit** | `fn.call(x)` / `fn.apply(x)` / `fn.bind(x)()` | `x`, forced regardless of how `fn` is otherwise called |
| **`new`** | `new Fn()` | the brand-new object being constructed |

When more than one rule could apply, higher precedence wins: `new obj.fn()` uses the `new` rule, not implicit binding, even though there's a dot. Explicit binding beats implicit too — `fn.call(x)` ignores whatever object `fn` happens to be a property of.

slides.subTitle: Borrowing functions, fixing `this`
slides.markdown:
All three force a specific `this`, and differ only in how they pass arguments and when they run:

```javascript
function greet(greeting) { return `${greeting}, ${this.name}`; }
const user = { name: "Priya" };

greet.call(user, "Hi");           // runs now, args listed individually: "Hi, Priya"
greet.apply(user, ["Hi"]);       // runs now, args as an array: "Hi, Priya"
const bound = greet.bind(user);  // returns a NEW function, doesn't run yet
bound("Hi");                      // "Hi, Priya" — this is permanently locked to user
```

`call`/`apply` **invoke immediately** with a forced `this`; `bind` **returns a new function** with `this` permanently fixed, safe to pass around and call later — which is exactly why `bind` is the standard fix for a detached callback losing its `this` (next slide).

"Borrowing" a function means calling someone else's method with your own object as `this` — `Array.prototype.slice.call(arrayLikeObject)` is the classic pre-spread example of turning an array-like `arguments` object into a real array.

slides.subTitle: Why they opt out of all four rules
slides.markdown:
Arrow functions don't have their own `this` binding at all. They don't participate in any of the four rules — instead, `this` inside an arrow function is resolved by the **scope chain**, exactly like a normal variable: it's whatever `this` was in the nearest enclosing non-arrow function (or the module/global scope, if there is none).

```javascript
const obj = {
  name: "Team",
  regular: function () { return this.name; },   // implicit binding — "Team"
  arrow: () => this.name,                          // lexical — this is the OUTER this, not obj
};
obj.regular(); // "Team"
obj.arrow();   // undefined (or global name, in sloppy mode) — this is NOT obj
```

This is why arrow functions **cannot** be rebound with `call`/`apply`/`bind` — there's no `this` slot on them to overwrite. Passing a `this` argument to an arrow function's `.call()` is silently ignored.

slides.sectionTitle: A decision tree for any call site
slides.markdown:
Given any function call, work through these questions in order — the first one that matches wins:

1. Is it an **arrow function**? → `this` = whatever the enclosing scope's `this` is (lexical, not one of the four rules).
2. Called with **`new`**? → `this` = the newly created object.
3. Called via **`.call()`/`.apply()`/`.bind()`**? → `this` = the explicitly passed object.
4. Called as **`obj.method()`**? → `this` = `obj`.
5. Called **bare**, `fn()`? → `this` = `undefined` (strict) or the global object (sloppy).

Memorizing this order matters because interview questions love mixing rules in one snippet — a method borrowed via `.call()` on an unrelated object, or a `new` call on a function stored as a property.
